name: partial-response
intent: Let the caller name the fields it actually wants, so the boundary returns a projected representation of the resource instead of the complete one - cutting payload size, serialization work and accidental data exposure without splitting the resource into per-client views.
problem: A boundary exposes resources that are large or expensive to compute, and different callers need different subsets of it: mobile clients want a slim reply, back-office tools want everything. Without a selection channel every new caller forces either a new endpoint or DTO, or an ever-growing default representation that all callers pay for - even though the caller already knows which fields it needs.
context: Remote and message boundaries where one logical resource serves many callers: HTTP/REST and gRPC APIs with a fields/read_mask channel (query parameter, header, system parameter or metadata), documents crossing an integration seam, and query languages whose request carries the selection set (GraphQL, OData $select, JSON:API sparse fieldsets). It assumes the resource has a stable field vocabulary (schema or descriptor) that requested paths can be validated against, and that the boundary - not the caller - owns defaults, permissions, cost limits and the versioning of the exposed field set.
benefits: Payload and serialization cost scale with what the caller asked for: fewer bytes on the wire, less encoding work, cheaper parsing on the client side.
One resource serves every caller: per-client slim endpoints and parallel DTO taxonomies disappear, and the same projection logic is reused across transports.
The response surface can grow without taxing existing callers - new fields join the default view and are fetched only by those who name them.
An explicit field vocabulary plus an allowlist turns accidental over-sharing into a reviewable artifact: exposure is one list to read, not a scattering of hand-built DTOs.
Composes with the rest of the boundary toolkit: the selector travels in the request, so caching, pagination, content negotiation and Tolerant Reader on the consumer side keep working.
tradeoffs: The response is no longer one shape but a family of shapes: clients, documentation and intermediaries must cope with request-dependent representations (JSON:API requires the intermediate-cache/Vary rules, and cache keys grow with the selection).
The default policy is a compatibility contract: changing it is a breaking change, and a partial-by-default resource degrades declarative clients that expect the complete representation (AIP-157).

Projection is often applied after full materialization (serialize the resource, then trim), so the compute saving can be much smaller than the byte saving unless the selection is pushed into the data layer.
Arbitrary masks multiply cache entries and invite complexity attacks - huge field lists, deep paths, expensive derived fields - so cost limits become part of the API contract.
Unknown or mistyped paths must either fail loudly or be dropped silently; both surprise someone, and dropping silently turns a typo into a quietly smaller payload.
Field selection intersects authorization but cannot replace it: a mask is a preference, never a permission, so a requested path must not widen what the caller may see.

participants.responsibility: States the field paths it needs - as a query parameter, header, read mask field, or selection set - and tolerates the projected shape; an absent selector means the documented default view.
Parses the requested paths into the resource's canonical field vocabulary and rejects unknown, unmappable or unauthorized paths before any work happens.

Produces the partial representation: filters in the serializer, prunes in the query, or trims the materialized document - keeping nesting, nullability and default-value semantics consistent with the full resource.
Owns the complete representation, the field vocabulary and the documented default view, and stays authoritative for computed, restricted and expensive fields.
Defines what an absent selector means - '*' unless documented otherwise, or a small enumerable set of named views (BASIC/FULL) when only a few permutations should be published.

use_cases: Public or multi-tenant APIs whose resources carry heavy sub-objects (profiles, documents, telemetry) where mobile and back-office callers need different slices of the same resource.
gRPC/Connect services that accept google.protobuf.FieldMask as a read mask (system parameter or gRPC metadata) and project the reply message before it leaves the process.
Integration seams that forward a document between systems: the receiving side names the fields it can process and the seam strips the rest, with Tolerant Reader guarding the incoming direction.
HTTP APIs following OData ($select, $expand) or JSON:API (fields[TYPE] sparse fieldsets), including per-type field sets inside compound documents.
Query-language boundaries (GraphQL, Caliban, Apollo clients) where the operation's selection set is the field list and the executor resolves only the selected fields.
Google Drive API clients use the `fields` parameter on file and change-list reads to request only the properties a sync or UI needs, reducing transfer and parsing work.
Google Compute Engine API clients use `fields` with nested selectors on list and get responses, keeping pagination metadata while trimming large resource payloads.
Microsoft Graph callers use OData `$select` (often alongside `$expand` and paging) to shape user, message or directory responses to the properties the workflow consumes.
avoid_when: The resource is small or cheap to produce: returning the whole representation, or a dedicated DTO for the one slim case, is simpler than a selection contract.
Exactly one fixed slice is ever needed: a dedicated endpoint or Mapper states it once instead of maintaining a mask language for a single consumer.
The selection would be unbounded (arbitrary graph paths): a small set of named views keeps the contract stable and the cache finite.
The consumer cannot act on the difference anyway - if the reply is stored or forwarded whole, a sender-side Content Filter or a slim default representation is less machinery.
The payload must stay byte-identical for signing, hashing or regulatory reasons regardless of the caller: partial responses break that guarantee.
anti_patterns: Passing the fields parameter straight into the ORM or query builder (SELECT assembled from caller input) - an injection and data-exfiltration hole wearing the pattern's name.
Partial-by-default with no way to ask for the complete resource, quietly degrading every client that assumes a full representation.
Using the mask as the authorization mechanism: fields are omitted because they were not requested, and permissions are never checked separately.
Serialize-the-whole-graph-then-delete on hot paths - the pattern's byte saving without its compute saving, plus allocation churn per request.
Rebuilding the same subset logic as a hand-written DTO per caller because the field vocabulary and default view were never written down as a contract.
design_principles: Interface segregation at the data level: a caller depends only on the fields it actually uses.
Explicit contract over implicit defaults: the field vocabulary, the default view and the error behaviour for unknown paths are documented and versioned.
Least data disclosure: send what was asked for, and keep permission filtering orthogonal to the request's preference.
Single source of truth: mask validation, serialization, documentation and permission rules all derive from one schema/descriptor.
Fail fast on invalid input instead of silently returning less - unknown paths are rejected at the boundary.
best_practices: Validate every requested path against the resource's canonical vocabulary and reject unknown paths with a clear error (protobuf FieldMask semantics: INVALID_ARGUMENT for unmappable paths).

Document the default explicitly - an absent selector returns the same shape the API would send if partial responses did not exist ('*' unless documented otherwise), and changing it is a breaking change.

Cap the selector: bound the number of paths, the nesting depth, and which expensive or derived fields may be requested; prefer a side channel (query parameter, header, metadata) over a per-request message field.
Project as early as the stack allows - column-pruned queries, typed DTOs, GraphQL resolvers, protobuf trimming - rather than materializing and then deleting.
Keep field selection and authorization independent; apply permission filtering after (or besides) the mask and never widen access because a field was requested.

Treat the field vocabulary and view definitions as versioned surface: additive changes only, never remove a field from a published view, and keep the intermediate-cache/Vary rules correct when responses vary by selector.
Test the projected shapes (one contract test per published view) rather than only the mask parser, and assert that unknown paths fail loudly.
